nodes.title: Generative AI and LLMs (AI-900 / AIF-C01): Key Ideas
nodes.content: Generative AI exams test conceptual understanding, not implementation. You need to know what a foundation model is, how Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) grounds a model in fresh knowledge, the spectrum of prompt engineering techniques, why hallucination happens, and what content safety guardrails do — framed for a business or cloud-architect audience.

flashcards.front: What is a foundation model and how does it differ from a task-specific model?
flashcards.back: A foundation model (GPT-4, Llama, Claude, Titan) is pretrained on massive general-purpose datasets and can perform many tasks via prompting or fine-tuning — one model, many uses. A task-specific model (sentiment classifier, image classifier) is trained end-to-end for one narrow task and cannot generalize. Foundation models are expensive to train but cheap to reuse; task-specific models are cheaper to fine-tune but brittle.

flashcards.front: RAG — what problem does it solve and how does it work?
flashcards.back: Retrieval-Augmented Generation solves the knowledge cutoff problem: the LLM's training data has a fixed date and doesn't include your proprietary documents. RAG adds a retrieval step: the query is used to fetch relevant chunks from an external store (vector DB, search index), which are injected into the prompt as context before the model generates a response. The model reasons over fresh retrieved content without retraining.

flashcards.front: Zero-shot vs few-shot vs chain-of-thought prompting — when do you use each?
flashcards.back: Zero-shot: give the model the task with no examples — fastest, works for well-defined instructions ('Summarize this text'). Few-shot: include 2–5 input/output examples in the prompt — guides format and style, better for classification or structured extraction. Chain-of-thought (CoT): ask the model to 'think step by step' — dramatically improves multi-step reasoning (math, logic) by making intermediate steps explicit before the final answer.

flashcards.front: Hallucination — what causes it and how do you mitigate it?
flashcards.back: Hallucination is when a generative model produces confident but factually incorrect output. Causes: the model pattern-matches from training data, filling gaps with plausible-sounding text when it lacks grounding. Mitigations: RAG (ground the model in retrieved facts), temperature lowering (less creative, more deterministic), citations (require the model to cite sources so outputs can be verified), human review for high-stakes content, fact-checking evaluation layers.

questions.q: You want an Azure OpenAI chat deployment to answer questions using your own private PDF policy documents, kept up to date with each release. Which pattern is recommended?
choices: Fine-tune the GPT model on the PDF text so it memorises the policy content
Paste the entire text of every policy PDF into the system prompt on each call
Store the PDF embeddings in Azure Blob storage and query them from the app directly
Index the PDFs in Azure AI Search and query them via the On Your Data feature
questions.explanation: The recommended Retrieval-Augmented Generation pattern is to chunk and embed the PDFs into an Azure AI Search index, then point the Azure OpenAI 'On Your Data' feature at that index so each query retrieves only the relevant passages. Fine-tuning bakes knowledge into model weights at training time — it teaches style and format rather than fresh facts, and re-running it on every release is slow, costly and still leaves the deployment stale between runs. Pasting every PDF into the system prompt burns tokens, raises latency and cost, and grounds nothing in retrieval. Storing raw embeddings in Blob storage gives you no vector index — every query would have to load and scan the whole file set from application code, whereas Azure AI Search is the vector-index-and-ranker Microsoft ships for exactly this scenario and On Your Data wires it into Azure OpenAI with grounded citations.

questions.q: By default, every Azure OpenAI deployment screens prompts and completions for harmful content across categories such as hate, violence, self-harm and sexual content. Which capability provides those built-in filters?
choices: Microsoft Defender for Cloud AI workload threat-protection rules
Azure AI Content Safety filters integrated into the deployment
Azure Policy initiatives scoped to generative AI resources
Microsoft Purview sensitivity labels applied to the model output
questions.explanation: Azure OpenAI deployments include Azure AI Content Safety filters by default; they score every prompt and completion for hate, violence, self-harm and sexual content against severity thresholds, and also provide Prompt Shields and protected-material detection. Microsoft Defender for Cloud — including its AI threat-protection plan — monitors deployment-level posture and flags attacks against the resource, but it does not perform inline classification of the content of each completion. Azure Policy enforces how Azure resources are configured (region, SKU, tagging), not what text a user sends through them. Microsoft Purview sensitivity labels classify and protect data assets for governance and DLP; they do not moderate harmful content in model request/response traffic.

questions.q: Your assistant must call live external APIs (weather, inventory) during a chat turn and weave the results back into its reply. Which Azure OpenAI capability orchestrates that pattern?
choices: Fine-tune the model on transcripts of previous real API responses
Embed the entire API reference documentation into every system prompt
Function (tool) calling, with a tools schema supplied in the request
Switch the deployment to the Assistants API code-interpreter tool
questions.explanation: Function (tool) calling lets the model emit a structured JSON call matching a tools schema you define in the request; your application then runs the real weather or inventory API and returns the result, which the model weaves into its reply. Fine-tuning on past transcripts bakes in stale snapshots of past responses and never invokes a live API at run time, so freshly changing inventory or weather would never surface. Embedding API reference docs in the prompt only describes the APIs to the model — it cannot invoke them and consumes tokens for context the model cannot act on. The Assistants API code-interpreter tool runs sandboxed Python for data analysis and visualisation, not arbitrary external HTTP API calls, so it is not the orchestrator for this pattern.

questions.q: A bank's Azure OpenAI assistant must never reveal another customer's data even if a user crafts an input designed to override the system instructions. Which Azure AI Content Safety capability is designed to detect that class of attack?
choices: Protected material detection, which flags known copyrighted text appearing in model completions
Prompt Shields, which screen incoming inputs for jailbreak and indirect prompt-injection patterns
Groundedness detection, which checks whether a completion is fully supported by the provided source data
Severity-based category filters, which score outputs for hate, violence, self-harm and sexual content
questions.explanation: Prompt Shields in Azure AI Content Safety are built to detect jailbreak attacks and indirect prompt-injection attempts that try to override system instructions, matching the described threat. Protected material detection flags known copyrighted text appearing in completions, which is a different content-risk class — it does not analyse user inputs for instruction-override attempts. Groundedness detection checks whether a response is fully supported by provided source data, which addresses hallucination rather than malicious input intent and would not catch a crafted user message until it had already steered the answer. Severity-based category filters score harmful-content categories such as hate, violence, self-harm and sexual content, not attempted manipulation of the system prompt.

nodes.title: Mixed exam topics: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Some exam objectives don't fit neatly into a single domain — they span protocols, tools, or concepts covered briefly in multiple sections. These cards treat each item as a stand-alone fact, the way an exam question presents it: one concept, one answer.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a hub, a switch, and a router?
flashcards.back: Hub: Layer 1, repeats every frame to all ports — all devices share bandwidth, collisions guaranteed. Switch: Layer 2, forwards frames using a MAC address table to only the destination port — full duplex, no collisions, each port gets full bandwidth. Router: Layer 3, makes forwarding decisions based on IP address, connects different networks. Hub is legacy; switches dominate LAN; routers are at network edges.

flashcards.front: What is RAID 5 and how many drives can it tolerate losing?
flashcards.back: RAID 5 stripes data and parity across at least 3 drives. Any single drive failure can be recovered by reconstructing missing data from the remaining drives and parity. It cannot tolerate 2 simultaneous drive failures. Effective capacity = (N-1) × drive size. Read performance is excellent; write requires parity recalculation. RAID 6 tolerates 2 failures using double parity.

flashcards.front: What does a proxy server do, and how does a forward proxy differ from a reverse proxy?
flashcards.back: Forward proxy: sits between clients and the internet on behalf of clients — used for content filtering, caching, and anonymizing outbound requests (the server sees the proxy's IP). Reverse proxy: sits in front of servers on behalf of the server — used for load balancing, SSL termination, caching, and hiding backend topology (the client sees the proxy's IP). Both intermediate HTTP, but they protect opposite sides.

flashcards.front: What is the purpose of a DMZ in network architecture?
flashcards.back: A demilitarized zone is a network segment between the untrusted internet and the trusted internal network, typically protected by two firewalls (or two interfaces on one firewall). Public-facing services (web, email, DNS) sit in the DMZ: internet can reach them but not the internal network; if the DMZ host is compromised, the inner firewall still blocks access to the internal LAN.

questions.q: You are deploying Azure AI capabilities for an enterprise app and need a single endpoint and key that authorise calls to Vision, Language, Speech and Translator with consolidated billing. Which resource type should you create?
choices: Four separate single-service resources, one per API, sharing a resource group
An Azure API Management gateway placed in front of four single-service resources
A multi-service Azure AI services resource exposing one shared endpoint and key
An Azure AI Foundry project on top of a hub, used as the inference endpoint
questions.explanation: A multi-service Azure AI services resource exposes a single endpoint and key that authorise Vision, Language, Speech, Translator and other Azure AI APIs, and rolls all usage onto one bill. Provisioning a separate single-service resource per API leaves you managing a distinct endpoint and key for each one and produces a separate line item per service. An API Management gateway can unify routing in front of those resources, but the single-service resources still exist, are still billed individually and still each have their own key — APIM adds a facade rather than consolidating the underlying service. An Azure AI Foundry project sits on top of a hub and organises models, connections and evaluations for AI development work — it does not itself serve Vision/Language/Speech/Translator inference; those calls still go to the underlying AI services resource that a Foundry hub connects to.

questions.q: Your team must rotate the access keys on a production Azure AI Language resource without interrupting client traffic that is already in flight. Which sequence is recommended?
choices: Regenerate the currently unused key, move all clients to it, then rotate the other
Regenerate both key1 and key2 simultaneously and redeploy every client in parallel
Regenerate the key clients are actively using and let them reconnect to the new value
Delete the resource and recreate it so brand-new keys are issued for both slots
questions.explanation: Azure AI resources expose two keys precisely so you can rotate with zero downtime: regenerate the key no client is currently using, migrate every client to that freshly rotated key, then regenerate the other so the previously active key is also retired. Regenerating both keys at once invalidates every live connection until all clients have been redeployed with new credentials, creating an authentication-error window. Regenerating the key clients are actively using breaks their in-flight calls immediately because that key value is invalidated the moment the regenerate operation completes — there is no overlap window for clients to swap to the new value. Deleting and recreating the resource also forces a brand-new resource ID and endpoint URL, so every client must be reconfigured for both the keys and the URL — that is a re-provision, not a key rotation.

questions.q: An Azure OpenAI chat application is being moved to production. Security requires that no API key be stored in the app, and that calls be authorized by the application's own Azure identity instead. Which approach should you implement?
choices: Assign the app a system-assigned managed identity and grant it the Cognitive Services OpenAI User role on the Azure OpenAI resource
Store key1 in Azure Key Vault and have the application fetch it at process startup using a vault connection string, then cache it
Inject key2 from the release pipeline into a runtime environment variable that the application reads at boot, refreshing on restart
Front the Azure OpenAI resource with Azure API Management and forward a subscription key from the gateway on every call
questions.explanation: Assigning the app a managed identity and granting it the Cognitive Services OpenAI User role on the Azure OpenAI resource removes keys entirely — the SDK acquires Microsoft Entra tokens automatically and authorizes calls by the app's own identity, which is the requirement. Fetching key1 from Azure Key Vault still relies on a key — the Azure OpenAI resource is authenticated by that key, not by the app's identity, and the app must additionally hold a vault-access secret. Injecting key2 as an environment variable both stores a key inside the runtime environment and exposes it to anyone who can read the process memory or pipeline logs. Placing Azure API Management in front authorizes the caller against the gateway with a subscription key, but APIM still has to authenticate to the Azure OpenAI resource downstream — typically with a key — so the requirement to eliminate keys is not met.

questions.q: Your chatbot must classify each user utterance into an intent and extract entities such as dates and locations from it. Which Azure AI Language feature should you use?
choices: Custom named entity recognition (custom NER) configured on its own
Sentiment analysis with opinion mining enabled on each utterance
Conversational language understanding (CLU) with a trained model
An orchestration workflow that routes utterances to other projects
questions.explanation: Conversational language understanding (CLU), the successor to LUIS, is purpose-built to predict an intent and extract entities from each utterance within a single trained model. Custom NER extracts named entities only and has no concept of intents, so it cannot classify the utterance itself — you would still need a second component to handle intent classification. Sentiment analysis with opinion mining returns sentiment polarity and aspect-level opinions; it does not learn intents or extract date/location entities. An orchestration workflow connects and routes between an underlying CLU project, custom question answering and other projects — it relies on a CLU project to do the intent-and-entity work rather than performing that classification itself.

questions.q: A multilingual support team must translate inbound chat messages into English in real time, automatically detecting the source language of each message without it being specified. Which Azure AI service capability handles this?
choices: Azure AI Language key phrase extraction followed by a separately built translation step over the extracted terms
Azure AI Speech speech translation configured for text-to-text conversion between chat messages in different languages
Azure AI Language abstractive summarization with the target language parameter set to English on every incoming call
Azure AI Translator text translation, with the 'from' parameter omitted to auto-detect the source language per call
questions.explanation: Azure AI Translator's text translation API detects the source language automatically when the 'from' parameter is omitted and returns the translated text in the requested target language, which fits real-time chat translation. Key phrase extraction surfaces salient terms from text; it does not translate, so an extra translation step would still be required and most of the original message would be discarded along the way. Speech translation operates on spoken audio input and produces translated speech or text from audio — it is the wrong modality for typed chat messages even when a text-to-text output mode exists. Abstractive summarization condenses text into a shorter form; it does not translate between languages even when a target-language parameter is supplied, so the output remains in the source language.

questions.q: You must extract entities like 'policy number' and 'claim ID' that are specific to your insurer's documents and do not exist in the prebuilt entity categories of Azure AI Language. Which feature should you use?
choices: Prebuilt named entity recognition (NER) filtered down to the Quantity and Number category outputs
Personally identifiable information (PII) detection with the redaction option enabled for outputs
Entity linking, which associates already-recognized entities with Wikipedia knowledge-base IDs
Custom named entity recognition (custom NER) trained on documents that your own team has labelled
questions.explanation: Custom NER lets you label your own documents and train a model to extract domain-specific entities such as policy number and claim ID that prebuilt categories do not cover. Prebuilt NER recognizes only Microsoft's fixed category set and cannot learn insurer-specific fields — filtering to Quantity or Number returns generic numeric spans, not labelled policy numbers or claim IDs. PII detection finds and can redact personal data types (names, emails, SSNs), not arbitrary custom business identifiers. Entity linking disambiguates already-recognized entities against a public knowledge base (Wikipedia/Wikidata) and does not extract new custom entity types.

questions.q: A retailer wants to detect and locate their own product SKUs inside shelf photographs using a small set of labelled images and a no-code training portal. Which Azure service fits best?
choices: Azure AI Vision Image Analysis 4.0 relying on its built-in generic object tagging
Azure AI Document Intelligence with a custom-trained field-extraction model
Azure AI Video Indexer with a custom-trained brand-and-object model applied to stills
An Azure AI Custom Vision object-detection project trained on the labelled images
questions.explanation: Azure AI Custom Vision lets you upload a small set of labelled images in a no-code portal and train an object-detection model that returns bounding boxes for your own product SKUs. Image Analysis 4.0 recognises only generic objects from Microsoft's prebuilt taxonomy — it cannot be taught new SKU classes from labelled examples. Document Intelligence extracts key-value fields from forms and documents and has no concept of locating products within a natural-scene shelf photo. Video Indexer is built for video timelines; while it does support custom brand insights, those run over video frames and faces/audio, not still product photographs, so it is the wrong modality for a SKU detector trained on labelled stills.

questions.q: A media archive needs to make spoken dialogue in thousands of recorded video files searchable, producing time-stamped transcripts plus detected topics and faces. Which Azure service is purpose-built for this?
choices: Azure AI Vision Image Analysis applied frame-by-frame to keyframes extracted from each clip
Azure AI Speech continuous recognition streamed against the audio track of every uploaded file
Azure AI Video Indexer running end-to-end across the audio and video tracks of a given file
Azure AI Document Intelligence Read model applied to subtitle sidecar files for each video
questions.explanation: Azure AI Video Indexer is the unified service that analyses audio and video together and ships time-stamped transcription, topic detection, face detection and a searchable index out of the box — exactly the archive scenario. Image Analysis on exported stills loses the audio track entirely and therefore cannot transcribe dialogue, so no transcript ever exists. Speech continuous recognition returns real-time text from an audio stream but delivers no video-level insights such as faces or topics — you would still need to bolt on face detection, topic extraction and a search index that Video Indexer already provides natively. The Document Intelligence Read model performs OCR on documents and depends on subtitle sidecar files that may not exist for raw recordings — and even when they do, it produces no face or topic insights.
